messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 76, Ramesh had spent most of his adult life as an electrician, the kind of man who was used to entering other people’s buildings with a toolbox, assessing a problem calmly, and fixing what could be fixed. The robbery happened after an evening service call, when he was leaving a small apartment complex with his work bag slung over one shoulder. In the narrow passage by the parking lot, two men closed in on him. What stayed with him was not only the shock of being grabbed and forced to hand over his wallet, but the sensory fragments that seemed burned in more deeply than the whole sequence: the press of bodies in too little space, one man lurching close with the stale smell of alcohol on his breath, and the abrupt, jerky movements of hands coming toward him before he could make sense of what was happening. He was not badly injured, but the incident left him shaken in a way he had not expected, especially because it happened during an ordinary workday and in a setting that had once felt routine.

In the months after, those fragments returned less as a coherent memory than as moments that seemed to invade the present. If he woke from a nightmare, he would come up abruptly, disoriented and already braced, as if the threat were still in the room with him. On jobs in apartment buildings or older commercial properties, he found himself studying hallways and stairwells for exits before focusing on the wiring. Crowded places became particularly difficult. When he had to stop at a hardware store and found the aisles full, the nearness of strangers on either side of him made his chest tighten and his attention narrow. A whiff of alcohol from a passerby could change the whole feel of the moment; he would stiffen immediately, his body acting before he could talk himself out of it.

These triggers had come to shape how dangerous the world felt to Ramesh. Waking from a nightmare did not stay contained to the night; once awake, he felt unable to settle, listening for sounds in the house and finding it much harder to believe he was safe after dark than during the day. In crowded places he was certain that ordinary proximity could shift in an instant into something predatory, and strangers approaching him even for mundane reasons—a question in a store, someone stepping toward him on a sidewalk—felt menacing before he had time to judge their intent. What frightened him most was how quickly sudden movements by other people put him on guard. A hand reaching across him at a counter, someone turning abruptly in a hallway, a person stepping out of an elevator too fast: each of these moments seemed to pull the robbery’s danger straight into the present, leaving him poised for harm.

This had begun to alter the texture of his days. Because so much of electrical work involves entering unfamiliar buildings and being around tenants, maintenance staff, and customers, he could not fully avoid the situations that unsettled him, but he moved through them differently now. He preferred daytime jobs and felt markedly less steady if a repair might run late into the evening. In apartment complexes he was especially tense near entrances, laundry rooms, and crowded corridors, where he disliked having people pass close behind him. If a client opened the door and he caught the smell of alcohol, even faintly, he found it difficult to concentrate until he had scanned the room and positioned himself where no one could approach unexpectedly. At home, his wife had noticed that if he woke from a bad dream, he would remain alert for hours, listening and checking locks, his whole manner watchful.

Ramesh finally agreed to seek help after recognizing how small his world had become internally, even when his routines outwardly remained intact. He was still working, still going where he had to go, but he no longer felt ordinary situations as ordinary. A crowded checkout line, a stranger stepping too close, the smell of alcohol on someone passing by, or the residue of a nightmare before dawn could all leave him feeling that danger was immediately near. He is most afraid that this constant readiness, especially at night, will become the permanent shape of the rest of his life. What he hopes for, said quietly, is not to erase what happened, but to be able to wake in his own home, finish a job, or walk through a store without feeling as though he must defend himself at any moment.
